top_cited_works.title: Helmholtz equation–least-squares method for reconstructing the acoustic pressure field
top_cited_works.venue: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
top_cited_works.abstract: A method using spherical wave expansion theory to reconstruct acoustic pressure field from a vibrating object is developed. The radiated acoustic pressures are obtained by means of an expansion of independent functions generated by the Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization with respect to the particular solutions to the Helmholtz equation on the vibrating surface under consideration. The coefficients associated with these independent functions are determined by requiring the assumed form of solution to satisfy the pressure boundary condition at the measurement points. The errors incurred in this process are minimized by the least-squares method. Once these coefficients are specified, the acoustic pressure at any point, including the source surface, is completely determined. In this paper, this method is used to reconstruct the surface acoustic pressures based on the measured acoustic pressure signals in the field. It is shown that this method can be applied to both separable and nonseparable geometries, and the solutions thus obtained are unique. However, the convergence may be worse for an elongated object subject to high-frequency excitations.

top_cited_works.title: On reconstruction of acoustic pressure fields using the Helmholtz equation least squares method
top_cited_works.venue: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
top_cited_works.abstract: This paper presents analyses and implementation of the reconstruction of acoustic pressure fields radiated from a general, three-dimensional complex vibrating structure using the Helmholtz equation least-squares (HELS) method. The structure under consideration emulates a full-size four-cylinder engine. To simulate sound radiation from a vibrating structure, harmonic excitations are assumed to act on arbitrarily selected surfaces. The resulting vibration responses are solved by the commercial FEM (finite element method) software I-DEAS. Once the normal component of the surface velocity distribution is determined, the surface acoustic pressures are calculated using standard boundary element method (BEM) codes. The radiated acoustic pressures over several planar surfaces at certain distances from the source are calculated by the Helmholtz integral formulation. These field pressures are taken as the input to the HELS formulation to reconstruct acoustic pressures on the entire source surface, as well as in the field. recent_works.title: A New Evidence Combination Method Based on Evidence Conflict Coefficient and its Application in Fault Diagnosis
recent_works.abstract: Dempster's combination rule faces challenges in handling conflict, particularly in multi-source data fusion tasks such as group decision-making and multi-attribute decision-making. When the evidence is highly conflicting, the classical Dempster's rule may produce results that contradict intuitive expectations. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel correlation coefficient to measure the differences among basic probability assignment (BPA) functions, along with a formal analysis of its theoretical properties. Furthermore, a new evidence conflict coefficient is defined and evaluated in comparison with existing conflict measurement methods. Based on this coefficient, an improved evidence combination method is developed. Experimental results show that the proposed method can effectively reduce the influence of conflicting evidence and yield more credible fusion outcomes. The approach is also applied to fault diagnosis, where its effectiveness and robustness under uncertain conditions are demonstrated.

recent_works.title: PBR-NeRF: Inverse Rendering with Physics-Based Neural Fields
recent_works.abstract: We tackle the ill-posed inverse rendering problem in 3D reconstruction with a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) approach informed by Physics-Based Rendering (PBR) theory, named PBR-NeRF. Our method addresses a key limitation in most NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting approaches: they estimate view-dependent appearance without modeling scene materials and illumination. To address this limitation, we present an inverse rendering (IR) model capable of jointly estimating scene geometry, materials, and illumination. Our model builds upon recent NeRF-based IR approaches, but crucially introduces two novel physics-based priors that better constrain the IR estimation. Our priors are rigorously formulated as intuitive loss terms and achieve state-of-the-art material estimation without compromising novel view synthesis quality. Our method is easily adaptable to other inverse rendering and 3D reconstruction frameworks that require material estimation. We demonstrate the importance of extending current neural rendering approaches to fully model scene properties beyond geometry and view-dependent appearance. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/s3anwu/pbrnerf.
